claim: Tuberculosis caused an estimated 1.3 million deaths in 2022.
source: With an estimated 1.3 million deaths in 2022, tuberculosis (TB) remains one of the deadliest infectious diseases in the world (WHO, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO 2023 report

claim: Human-adapted MTBC strains are classified into 10 phylogenetic lineages (L1 to L10).
source: Human‐adapted MTBC strains are classified into 10 phylogenetic lineages (L1 to L10), which are considered 'ancestral' (L1 and L5 to L10) or 'modern' (L2 to L4) based on the presence or absence of the TbD1 genomic region (Brosch et al., 2002; Comas et al., 2013; Coscolla et al., 2021; Guyeux et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature

claim: MTBC lineages are classified as 'ancestral' (L1 and L5 to L10) or 'modern' (L2 to L4) based on the presence or absence of the TbD1 genomic region.
source: Human‐adapted MTBC strains are classified into 10 phylogenetic lineages (L1 to L10), which are considered 'ancestral' (L1 and L5 to L10) or 'modern' (L2 to L4) based on the presence or absence of the TbD1 genomic region (Brosch et al., 2002; Comas et al., 2013; Coscolla et al., 2021; Guyeux et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature

claim: L1 to L4 lineages are responsible for most TB cases worldwide.
source: Among these lineages, L1 to L4 are responsible for most of the TB cases worldwide, with less prevalent lineages restricted to specific African regions.
evidence: Statement based on established epidemiological knowledge

claim: Less prevalent MTBC lineages are restricted to specific African regions.
source: Among these lineages, L1 to L4 are responsible for most of the TB cases worldwide, with less prevalent lineages restricted to specific African regions.
evidence: Statement based on established epidemiological knowledge

claim: Local adaptation to specific human hosts has been proposed to support the uneven phylogeographic distribution and disease burden of different MTBC lineages.
source: Local adaptation to specific human hosts has been proposed to support this uneven phylogeographic distribution and disease burden of different MTBC lineages (Gagneux et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gagneux et al., 2006

claim: The clinical implications of MTBC genetic diversity on vaccine efficacy remain unclear.
source: Irrespective of the underlying reason for this phylogeographic population structure, the clinical implications of MTBC genetic diversity, particularly on vaccine efficacy, remain unclear (Pérez et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pérez et al., 2020

claim: Ancestral L1 has been associated with higher rates of extrapulmonary TB.
source: For example, several reports have described an association between ancestral L1 and higher rates of extrapulmonary TB (Caws et al., 2008; Click et al., 2012; Saelens et al., 2022; Séraphin et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior clinical studies

claim: Strains belonging to ancestral lineages display a lower capacity to transmit compared to strains from modern lineages L2 and L4.
source: Moreover, strains belonging to ancestral lineages display a lower capacity to transmit compared to strains from the modern lineages L2 and L4 (Caws et al., 2008; Guerra-Assunção et al., 2015; Nebenzahl-Guimaraes et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior studies

claim: South Indian MTBC isolates were less virulent than strains from British patients in the guinea pig model in the 1960s.
source: The first experimental clues regarding the phenotypic consequences of strain genetic variation in the MTBC date from the 1960s with the observation that South Indian isolates were less virulent than strains from British patients in the guinea pig model (Mitchison et al., 1960).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mitchison et al., 1960

claim: Modern lineages (L2 to L4) proliferated significantly more than ancestral ones (L1 and L5) in in vitro granulomas.
source: Modern lineages (L2 to L4) proliferated significantly more than ancestral ones (L1 and L5) did (median rates 52.1 [modern] vs. 27.2 [ancestral]) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The growth rate of L2 tended to be higher than that of other modern lineages (L3 and L4).
source: Stratification of the data by lineage revealed that the growth rate of L2 tended to be higher than that of the other modern lineages (median rates 76.0 [L2] vs. 45.1 [L3] and 53.7 [L4]) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Substantial intra-lineage heterogeneity in growth rate was observed, particularly within L1 and L2.
source: Nevertheless, substantial intra-lineage heterogeneity could be observed, particularly within L1 and L2 (coefficients of variation 84.4% [L1] and 66.0% [L2] vs. 32.6% [L3], 34.6% [L4], and 31.9% [L5]).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Strain L1B displayed a high growth rate comparable to that of most strains belonging to modern lineages.
source: As depicted in Figure 1C, the lower virulence observed for ancestral lineages in general was contrasted by strain L1B that displayed a high growth rate (median 64.7) comparable to that of most strains belonging to modern lineages.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: L2 Beijing strains (L2B and L2C) exhibited a hyper-virulent phenotype.
source: Moreover, while L2 Beijing strains (L2B and L2C) exhibited a characteristic hyper-virulent phenotype (median rates 76.0 and 111.6, respectively), the proto-Beijing L2A was one of the most attenuated strains (median 14.7).
evidence: Supported by experimental data on growth rates

claim: The proto-Beijing L2A was one of the most attenuated strains.
source: Moreover, while L2 Beijing strains (L2B and L2C) exhibited a characteristic hyper-virulent phenotype (median rates 76.0 and 111.6, respectively), the proto-Beijing L2A was one of the most attenuated strains (median 14.7).
evidence: Supported by experimental data on growth rates

claim: The reference strain H37Rv displayed a lower growth rate than any of the evaluated L4 clinical isolates.
source: Noteworthy, the reference strain H37Rv, belonging to L4, displayed a lower growth rate than any of the evaluated L4 clinical isolates.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing H37Rv to L4 clinical isolates

claim: A constitutive overexpression of dosR in L2 Beijing strains has been proposed to contribute to their enhanced virulence and transmissibility.
source: A constitutive overexpression of dosR in L2 Beijing strains has been proposed to contribute to their enhanced virulence and transmissibility (Reed et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reed et al., 2007

claim: A genomic duplication including the DosR operon and a synonymous SNP within Rv3134c have been linked to increased expression of the DosR regulon.
source: A genomic duplication including the DosR operon and a synonymous SNP within Rv3134c, which generates an alternative transcriptional start site, have been linked to this increased expression of the DosR regulon (Domenech et al., 2010; Domenech et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Domenech et al., 2010 and 2017

claim: The in vitro granuloma model generates a hypoxic environment leading to dormant-like MTBC features.
source: A hallmark of our in vitro granuloma model resides in the generation of a hypoxic environment leading to dormant-like MTBC features such as the induction of DosR-regulated genes and the loss of acid-fastness and accumulation of triacylglycerides, which can be quantified by differential Auramine-O (Au)/Nile red (NR) fluorescent staining (Arbués et al., 2020a; Arbués et al., 2021; Kapoor et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work by the authors and others

claim: L2 strains exhibited an increased propensity to accumulate triacylglycerides compared to L1 and L4.
source: Nonetheless, L2 strains exhibited an increased propensity to accumulate triacylglycerides (median dormancy ratio 1.30; p=0.072 vs. L1 and p<0.05 vs. L4 by corrected Dunn's multiple comparisons test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis

claim: L3 bacilli seemed more prone to remain in a metabolically active state compared to bacteria belonging to other lineages.
source: By contrast, L3 bacilli seemed more prone to remain in a metabolically active state in comparison to bacteria belonging to the other lineages (median dormancy ratio 0.54; p=0.072 vs. L5 by corrected Dunn's multiple comparisons test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis

claim: The ratio between dormant-like and metabolically active bacilli showed no correlation with the respective growth rate of individual MTBC strains.
source: Interestingly, the ratio between dormant-like and metabolically active bacilli showed no correlation with the respective growth rate of the individual MTBC strains (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C

claim: All MTBC strains induced the formation of in vitro granulomas in variable numbers, shapes, and sizes.
source: While uninfected (UI) peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) did not lead to significant aggregation, all MTBC strains induced the formation of in vitro granulomas in variable numbers, shapes, and sizes (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Strains L1A, L2A, and L5B displayed a tendency to induce more aggregates per field with a less circular shape.
source: Strains L1A, L2A, and L5B displayed a tendency to induce more aggregates per field (median 42.5 [L1A], 40 [L2A], and 31.5 [L5B] vs. 22 [across all strains]) that were characterized by a less circular shape (i.e. higher aspect ratio) (median aspect ratios 1.38 [L1A], 1.35 [L2A], and 1.33 [L5B] vs. 1.25 [across all strains]) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative microscopy data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B

claim: L3 and L4 strains triggered the formation of markedly larger granulomas.
source: By contrast, L3 and L4 strains triggered the formation of markedly larger granulomas (median average area per granuloma in μm2: 6586.4 [L3] and 7800 [L4] vs. 3377.8 [L1], 5199.2 [L2] and 4638.4 [L5]) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative microscopy data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C

claim: Infection with modern lineages, especially L3 and L4, led to granulomatous responses with significantly higher aggregate formation scores.
source: Infection with modern lineages, especially L3 and L4, led to granulomatous responses with significantly higher scores (median scores 205.6 [L2], 374.8 [L3], and 290.2 [L4] vs. 107.2 [L1] and 130.2 [L5]) (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The aggregate formation score showed a significant positive correlation with the respective strain growth rate.
source: Interestingly, the aggregate formation score showed a significant positive correlation with the respective strain growth rate (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3D

claim: Apoptosis of infected macrophages drives early dissemination and granuloma formation.
source: It has been reported that apoptosis of infected macrophages drives early dissemination and granuloma formation (Aguilo et al., 2013; Davis and Ramakrishnan, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: L1A and L2A strains exhibited reduced induction of macrophage apoptosis.
source: By contrast, L1A and L2A strains, which were associated with the lowest growth rates and granulomatous responses, also exhibited a reduced induction of macrophage apoptosis (median percentages 29.6% and 30.2%, respectively); while L2C, the most virulent strain, induced the highest apoptosis levels (median percentage of apoptotic macrophages 49.4%).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data

claim: L2C, the most virulent strain, induced the highest apoptosis levels.
source: By contrast, L1A and L2A strains, which were associated with the lowest growth rates and granulomatous responses, also exhibited a reduced induction of macrophage apoptosis (median percentages 29.6% and 30.2%, respectively); while L2C, the most virulent strain, induced the highest apoptosis levels (median percentage of apoptotic macrophages 49.4%).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data

claim: The percentage of apoptotic macrophages showed a significant positive correlation with the replication rate of the respective infecting MTBC strain.
source: In fact, the percentage of apoptotic macrophages showed a significant positive correlation with the replication rate of the respective infecting MTBC strain (Figure 4B) as well as with aggregate formation scores (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B and 4C

claim: The percentage of apoptotic macrophages showed a significant positive correlation with aggregate formation scores.
source: In fact, the percentage of apoptotic macrophages showed a significant positive correlation with the replication rate of the respective infecting MTBC strain (Figure 4B) as well as with aggregate formation scores (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: Granulomatous responses elicited by L1A, L2A, and both L5 strains entailed marked CD4 T cell proliferation.
source: As depicted in Figure 5B, granulomatous responses elicited by L1A, L2A, and both L5 strains entailed marked CD4 T cell proliferation.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Ancestral lineages were the most potent inducers of T cell activation markers.
source: Overall, ancestral lineages were the most potent inducers of all the aforementioned T cell populations (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A), with CD38-expressing CD4 T cells constituting the most differentially induced population (median scaled frequencies 1.21 [ancestral] vs. 0.79 [modern]).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A

claim: Among modern lineages, L4 induced the strongest T cell activation.
source: Among modern lineages, L4 induced the strongest T cell activation (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 3B), which actually was not statistically different from that elicited by ancestral strains (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B

claim: CD4 T cell proliferation and all activation markers exhibited significant, moderate to strong, negative correlations with MTBC strain growth rate.
source: CD4 T cell proliferation as well as all expression of all activation markers exhibited significant, moderate to strong, negative correlations with MTBC strain growth rate, with the expression of CD38 resulting in the strongest coefficient.
evidence: Supported by Spearman's correlation analysis with multiple testing correction

claim: Activation of CD8 T cells, determined by the expression of either CD38 or CD69, was significantly associated with hampered mycobacterial proliferation.
source: Activation of CD8 T cells, determined by the expression of either CD38 or CD69, was also significantly associated with a hampered mycobacterial proliferation.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis

claim: A significant negative correlation exists between macrophage apoptosis induction and activated CD4 T cells expressing CD38.
source: Shedding light on what distinguishes granulomas that are protective from those that support bacterial growth, a significant negative correlation between macrophage apoptosis induction and T cell activation can be observed specifically with activated CD4 T cells expressing CD38 (rS = –0.36, p<0.05) or CD69 (rS = –0.40, p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis

claim: A significant negative correlation exists between macrophage apoptosis induction and activated CD4 T cells expressing CD69.
source: Shedding light on what distinguishes granulomas that are protective from those that support bacterial growth, a significant negative correlation between macrophage apoptosis induction and T cell activation can be observed specifically with activated CD4 T cells expressing CD38 (rS = –0.36, p<0.05) or CD69 (rS = –0.40, p<0.01).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis

claim: L4 and, to a lesser extent, L3 induced a significantly higher secretion of IL-1β on day 1 post-infection.
source: L4 and, to a lesser extent, L3 induced a significantly higher secretion of IL-1β on day 1 post-infection (median scaled responses 1.54 [L4] and 1.31 [L3] vs. 0.55 [L1], 0.94 [L2], and 0.89 [L5]) (Figure 6C, left).
evidence: Supported by multiplex bead-based immunoassay data shown in Figure 6C

claim: The IL-1β response on day 1 post-infection showed a moderate positive correlation with aggregate formation score.
source: Interestingly, the IL-1β response on day 1 post-infection showed a moderate positive correlation with aggregate formation score (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6D

claim: Neutralization of IL-1β significantly decreased the aggregate formation score of granulomas generated by high IL-1β inducer strain L4C.
source: Neutralization significantly decreased the score of granulomas generated by high IL-1β inducer strain L4C, whereas it had no effect on granulomas associated with low IL-1β inducer strain L1A, thereby establishing a cause-effect relationship between these two phenotypes (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by experimental blocking data shown in Figure 6E

claim: IL-13 was preferentially induced in the context of infection with modern lineages compared to ancestral lineages.
source: Moreover, we found that the CD4 T helper 2 cytokine IL-13 was preferentially induced in the context of infection with modern lineages compared to ancestral lineages (median scaled responses 1.18 [modern] vs. 0.78 [ancestral]) (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by multiplex bead-based immunoassay data shown in Figure 6F

claim: Induction of CXCL9 secretion on day 1 post-infection was associated with reduced MTBC bacterial proliferation.
source: While we found no significant correlation for IFN-γ, induction of CXCL9 secretion on day 1 post-infection, and granzyme B as well as TNF on day 8 post-infection were associated with a reduced MTBC bacterial proliferation (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6G

claim: Granzyme B secretion on day 8 post-infection was associated with reduced MTBC bacterial proliferation.
source: While we found no significant correlation for IFN-γ, induction of CXCL9 secretion on day 1 post-infection, and granzyme B as well as TNF on day 8 post-infection were associated with a reduced MTBC bacterial proliferation (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6G

claim: TNF secretion on day 8 post-infection was associated with reduced MTBC bacterial proliferation.
source: While we found no significant correlation for IFN-γ, induction of CXCL9 secretion on day 1 post-infection, and granzyme B as well as TNF on day 8 post-infection were associated with a reduced MTBC bacterial proliferation (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6G

claim: Blocking of CXCL9 during infection did not impact bacterial load of either high or low CXCL9 inducer strains.
source: However, blocking of CXCL9 during the infection failed to confirm causality since it did not impact bacterial load of either the high CXCL9 inducer strain L1A or the low CXCL9 inducer strain L2C (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by experimental blocking data shown in Figure 6H

claim: Modern Beijing strains exhibited enhanced virulence in mice compared to those with an ancestral genotype.
source: This is also consistent with prior studies showing that modern Beijing strains exhibited enhanced virulence in mice compared to those with an ancestral genotype (Ribeiro et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ribeiro et al., 2014

claim: L2 Beijing strains were poor inducers of T cell activation and pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: Likewise, we found that both L2 Beijing strains were poor inducers of T cell activation and pro-inflammatory cytokines.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study

claim: The high replication rate of L4 strains was accompanied by significant T cell activation and high levels of IFN-γ.
source: By contrast, we found the high replication rate of L4 strains to be accompanied by a significant T cell activation and high levels of IFN-γ.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study

claim: Higher IL-1β levels trigger autophagy, but L4 isolates evade subsequent lysosomal degradation.
source: Romagnoli and collaborators showed that higher IL-1β levels trigger autophagy; however, L4 isolates evade subsequent lysosomal degradation (Romagnoli et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Romagnoli et al., 2018

claim: Increased IL-1β levels in bronchoalveolar lavage or serum of TB patients have been associated with presence of cavities and higher bacterial loads in sputum.
source: Despite its protective role (Mayer-Barber et al., 2010), increased IL-1β levels in the bronchoalveolar lavage or serum of TB patients have been associated with presence of cavities and higher bacterial loads in sputum (Sigal et al., 2017; Tsao et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sigal et al., 2017 and Tsao et al., 2000

claim: High transmission strains induced an increased expression of IL-1β in the lungs of infected mice compared to low transmission ones.
source: Consonantly, high transmission strains induced an increased expression of IL-1β in the lungs of infected mice compared to low transmission ones (Lovey et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lovey et al., 2022

claim: L3 was characterized by a tendency to preferentially remain in a metabolically active state, in contrast with the increased propensity of L2 to enter dormancy.
source: Lastly, L3 was characterized by a tendency to preferentially remain in a metabolically active state, in contrast with the increased propensity of L2 to enter dormancy, which was previously reported under standard culture conditions in broth (Reed et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study and citation to Reed et al., 2007

claim: There was no correlation between the propensity to switch into a dormant-like state and virulence across MTBC lineages.
source: In line with this, our results show that even in the context of hypoxic granulomatous responses—which are lacking in the mouse model—there was no correlation between the propensity to switch into a dormant-like state and virulence, as reflected in bacterial burden in our model, across MTBC lineages.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study

claim: T cells are essential for immunity against the MTBC.
source: T cells are essential for immunity against the MTBC (Kaufmann, 2002) hence, it is unsurprising that the level of CD4 and CD8 T cell activation inversely correlated with mycobacterial growth rate.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kaufmann, 2002 and established immunological knowledge

claim: The level of CD4 and CD8 T cell activation inversely correlated with mycobacterial growth rate.
source: T cells are essential for immunity against the MTBC (Kaufmann, 2002) hence, it is unsurprising that the level of CD4 and CD8 T cell activation inversely correlated with mycobacterial growth rate.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study

claim: The prominent protective role of TNF in TB is well known.
source: Among the identified soluble factors, the prominent protective role of TNF in TB is well known (Flynn et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Flynn et al., 1995 and established knowledge

claim: CXCL9's paradigmatic function is directing the migration of CXCR3-expressing cells.
source: CXCL9's paradigmatic function is directing the migration of CXCR3-expressing cells (i.e. T helper 1 CD4 T cells, effector CD8 T cells, and natural killer cells) (Groom and Luster, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Groom and Luster, 2011

claim: CXCL9 has attracted attention as potential biomarker for TB diagnosis and treatment monitoring.
source: CXCL9 has attracted attention as potential biomarker for TB diagnosis and treatment monitoring (Ambreen et al., 2021; Uzorka et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ambreen et al., 2021 and Uzorka et al., 2022

claim: Protective vaccination in mice triggered the production of chemokines, including CXCL9, in the lung and associated recruitment of CXCR3+ CD4 T cells.
source: Protective vaccination in mice triggered the production of chemokines, including CXCL9, in the lung and associated recruitment of CXCR3+ CD4 T cells (Khader et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Khader et al., 2007

claim: Increased densities of CXCR3+ CD4 T cells were found in the lungs of latently infected NHPs relative to those with active TB.
source: In addition, increased densities of CXCR3+ CD4 T cells were found in the lungs of latently infected NHPs relative to those with active TB (Shanmugasundaram et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shanmugasundaram et al., 2020

claim: CXCL9 has been reported as a new marker of trained immunity in mycobacterial growth inhibition assays.
source: CXCL9 has also been reported as a new marker of trained immunity in mycobacterial growth inhibition assays (Joosten et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Joosten et al., 2018

claim: In NHPs, low burden granulomas were associated with a higher proportion of a T/NK cell cluster expressing granzyme B.
source: In NHPs, low burden granulomas were associated with a higher proportion of a T/NK cell cluster expressing granzyme B (Gideon et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gideon et al., 2022

claim: Individuals with latent TB infection exhibited increased expression of granzyme B in activated NK cells.
source: Furthermore, individuals with latent TB infection exhibited increased expression of granzyme B in activated NK cells (Esaulova et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Esaulova et al., 2021

claim: TB vaccine trials demonstrated that induction of strong IFN-γ responses does not translate into enhanced protection.
source: Our finding is supported by TB vaccine trials demonstrating that induction of strong IFN-γ responses does not translate into enhanced protection (Tameris et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tameris et al., 2013

claim: The in vitro granuloma model lacks granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, and mast cells).
source: The model encompasses all PBMC-derived cell types involved in TB immune responses, but lacks granulocytes (i.e. neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, and mast cells).
evidence: Statement about the model's composition

claim: Neutrophils play a pathogenic role in TB by providing a permissive environment for mycobacterial replication.
source: Consequently, the interface between the MTBC strains and neutrophils—which play a pathogenic role in TB by providing a permissive environment for mycobacterial replication (Andrews et al., 2024; Gideon et al., 2019; Lowe et al., 2013)—could not be investigated.
evidence: Supported by citations to Andrews et al., 2024, Gideon et al., 2019, and Lowe et al., 2013

claim: MTBC isolates display a range of growth rates correlating with the induction of macrophage apoptosis and the extent of the resulting granulomatous structures.
source: We show that MTBC isolates display a range of growth rates correlating with the induction of macrophage apoptosis and the extent of the resulting granulomatous structures.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the study

claim: TbD1 deletion significantly increases MTB virulence in relevant infection models.
source: Actually, in an elegant work using recombinant strains, Bottai and colleagues demonstrated that TbD1 deletion significantly increases MTB virulence in relevant infection models (Bottai et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bottai et al., 2020

claim: L1 is found in countries along the rim of the Indian Ocean.
source: L1 is found in countries along the rim of the Indian Ocean.
evidence: Statement based on established epidemiological knowledge

claim: L1 exhibits a highly diverse population structure.
source: This phenotypic variability may be a reflection of the highly diverse population structure exhibited by this lineage (Netikul et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Netikul et al., 2021

claim: The contribution of L1 to the global TB pandemic is generally undervalued.
source: However, a recent report revealed that the contribution of L1 to the global TB pandemic is generally undervalued (Netikul et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Netikul et al., 2021

claim: L1 was estimated to account for 28% of the total TB cases.
source: Due to its prevalence in countries with the highest TB incidence, L1 was estimated to account for 28% of the total TB cases.
evidence: Supported by epidemiological data

claim: L5 is geographically restricted to West Africa.
source: Meanwhile, L5, previously known as Mycobacterium africanum 1, is geographically restricted to West Africa.
evidence: Statement based on established epidemiological knowledge

claim: In Ghana, infection by L5 has been associated with the Ewe ethnic group.
source: In Ghana, infection by L5 has been associated with the Ewe ethnic group (Asante-Poku et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Asante-Poku et al., 2015

claim: L5 strains displayed lower growth in macrophages from the Akan ethnic group.
source: L5 strains displayed lower growth in macrophages from the Akan ethnic group; still, proliferation in Ewe's macrophages was comparable to that of L4 isolates (Osei-Wusu et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Osei-Wusu et al., 2023

claim: Modern Beijing strains exhibited enhanced virulence in mice compared to those with an ancestral genotype.
source: This is also consistent with prior studies showing that modern Beijing strains exhibited enhanced virulence in mice compared to those with an ancestral genotype (Ribeiro et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ribeiro et al., 2014

claim: L2 Beijing strains inhibit the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines.
source: One previously identified mechanism contributing to the hyper-virulent phenotype of L2 Beijing strains is the inhibition of the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Reed et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Reed et al., 2004 and Wang et al., 2010

claim: MTBC strain CDC1551 was characterized by very large skin test responses in infected subjects and a robust pro-inflammatory immune response in mice and in human monocytes.
source: These data are consistent with the fact that MTBC strain CDC1551, responsible for one of the most studied L4 outbreaks, was characterized by very large skin test responses in infected subjects and a robust pro-inflammatory immune response in mice and in human monocytes (Manca et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Manca et al., 1999

claim: A robust T cell activation characterized by an early CXCL9 detection and higher levels of TNF and granzyme B may orchestrate the control of mycobacterial growth.
source: Altogether, these results convey that a robust T cell activation characterized by an early CXCL9 detection and higher levels of TNF and granzyme B may orchestrate the control of mycobacterial growth.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation data presented in the study

claim: Different virulence strategies and protective immune traits associate with MTBC genetic diversity at lineage and strain level.
source: Taken together, our data indicate that different virulence strategies and protective immune traits associate with MTBC genetic diversity at lineage and strain level.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on all experimental data from the study

claim: Effective treatments and vaccines need to be tailored to account for MTBC strain diversity.
source: In summary, our investigation exposed various features that associate with certain MTBC lineages and/or strains, thereby reinforcing the concept that effective treatments and vaccines need to be tailored.
evidence: Inference based on the findings of strain diversity
